- The price the run reported is compared against what the collection holds afterwards, and they

description:
The priced, named, approvable decision shipped on 2026-08-27: a run reports each note whose
note-type shrink would destroy cards, states what that costs THAT note in cards and reviews,
and applies exactly one of them when named with --approve <handle>.

Its real path has never run. Every test of it is against the in-memory collection, and every
use of it has been a dry run. The code that actually moves a note and strands a card has not
executed once.
design:
WHY THIS IS WORTH ITS OWN ITEM RATHER THAN WAITING FOR AN OCCASION.

The feature exists to protect review history. A defect in it is not a wrong answer on a screen;
it is cards destroyed with their history, in a collection, silently. That is the one failure
this project cannot walk back.

Until 2026-08-28 it was doubly unverified: the in-memory collection it is tested against
computed a note's card count FROM THE NOTE TYPE'S NAME rather than from the spec it was handed,
so the double was known to be wrong about precisely the quantity the feature reports. That is
fixed. What remains is narrow and therefore worth closing while it is narrow.

HOW: in a throwaway profile, never User 1 and never the live obsidian-anki-srs profile. Create a
note on a three-template type, review a card so it has history, narrow its marker, run the sync,
read the reported price, approve it by name, then check what Anki actually holds - including
after Tools > Check Database, because orphaned and destroyed look identical without it.

WHAT WOULD MAKE IT A FAILURE: the reported price disagreeing with what the collection loses, in
either direction. Reporting more than it destroys erodes trust in the number; reporting less
destroys history the author did not agree to spend.
title: Exercise --approve against a real collection, once

description:
Anki's own Change Note Type dialogue lets a person map templates explicitly — say which old template becomes which new one — and that is the one real advantage the tool's refusal advice has over the tool itself: it can only tell the author to go and do it by hand. If AnkiConnect exposes the same mapping, the tool can offer what the dialogue offers instead of pointing at it.

UNMEASURED. Nothing waits on it: the priced-approval path shipped without it, and this would improve the advice rather than unblock anything. Recorded because it was named in REVIEW-QUEUE as a thing to measure and would otherwise have been lost when that section was cut.

The check is reading the add-on's own apiReflect action list, which is how the absence of a card-deleting action was established on 2026-08-27.
title: Check whether AnkiConnect exposes template mapping on a note-type change

description:
RULED BY MARC, 2026-09-01. Asked whether `docs/reference/LEARNING-MODEL.md` belongs in
`reference/`, he chose neither that nor `design/`: "Needs its own kind — neither reference nor
design. It is the pedagogy the whole tool serves, upstream of any of it. The four-directory scheme
has no slot, and forcing it into one is what makes it read as prescription rather than as the
thinking behind the design."

WHY THE CURRENT PLACEMENT MISLEADS. `docs/README.md` reserves `reference/` for "how the tool works
NOW". The learning model describes spacing, interleaving, two queues, what a card should test, and
a graduation rule Marc has since called "just a rough idea ... an order of magnitude". Almost none
of it is shipped behaviour, and much of what it prescribes appears in `CARD-MODEL.md`'s own
"Deliberately deferred" list. Filed as reference, its provisional thinking reads as settled fact —
which is exactly how the one-week horizon came to carry a rejected feature area.

WHAT THE NEW KIND IS FOR. Documents that are UPSTREAM of the tool: the pedagogy it serves, the
preferences it satisfies, the reasons any of it exists. They cannot go stale against the code
because they make no claim about it — which is a different reason from `design/`'s (a decision is a
historical fact) and from `findings/`'s (a measurement is true of its moment).

NOT SETTLED HERE, and worth deciding together:
  - The name of the directory. It is the "why", where `reference/` is the "what" and `design/` the
    "why this way".
  - Whether `REQUIREMENTS.md` is the same kind. It states what Marc wants and why, with an evidence
    class per claim — also upstream, also not a description of the tool. If it is, the new
    directory has two members and `reference/` shrinks to the two documents that really do describe
    current behaviour.
  - Whether the new kind takes the beads query line. Probably yes: `LEARNING-MODEL.md` already has
    open questions, and they should be findable.
title: The four-document scheme has no kind for the thinking upstream of the tool

description:
25. **THE ANKI-FACING SEAM IS STRINGLY TYPED, AND THAT IS A MODELLING GAP RATHER THAN A STYLE ONE.**
    _Recorded 2026-08-27. Supersedes item 6, which ranked it "possibly not worth doing"._

    **The three parts, in order of how much they hide.**

    - **A field has no ROLE.** Nothing anywhere says that `Front` on `Obsidian Basic` plays the part
      `Descriptor` plays on `Obsidian Concept-Descriptor`. The word *role* appears **zero times**
      across the eleven markdown documents in this repository. So when a note sits on a note type
      the vault did not ask for, the tool can say a name differs and can say nothing whatever about
      what the note's fields currently MEAN.
    - **A note type is a `String` on both sides** — `ObservedNote.noteType` and
      `CardSpec.noteTypeName` — compared with `!=`. The comparison is right and the type is a bag
      of characters at the point where the domain is richest.
    - **Field names are strings in four places that must agree and are tied together only by
      tests**: the manifests under `resources/note-types/`, the template text (which references
      them in Anki's own language, type-checked by nothing), `CardSpec.fields`, and
      `NoteTypeInstall`'s drift comparison.

    **The counterexample that got it re-ranked.** A heading marked `#flashcard/cdd/2way` sat on
    `Obsidian Basic (and reversed card)` with its DESCRIPTOR in the `Front` slot and its CONCEPT
    demoted to `Context`. Card 2 therefore showed the description and asked for the descriptor —
    not one of the three questions `cdd/2way` promises. Marc reviewed it repeatedly. The run
    reported the mismatch as a note-type name difference, which is all it could say, and told him
    "Leaving them is safe" — true about his data and false about his reviews.

    _The underlying note-type mismatch is fixed (item 16) and the gate is widened. What is NOT
    fixed is that the tool had no vocabulary for the state, which is why it could not describe it._

    **A FOURTH PART, ADDED 2026-08-29 AFTER IT COST SOMETHING.** A note's FIELD SET travels as
    `Vector[(String, String)]` — measured, 23 production signatures and 11 in tests: the card
    spec, three `SyncAction` cases, the `Anki` port, both implementations, the wire client, and
    the card-generation rules.

    **What it cost.** The in-memory collection let `addNote` create a note holding FEWER fields
    than its note type declares — a state Anki cannot represent, since a note's fields ARE its
    type's list and adding a field to a type gives every existing note that field, empty. A test
    then modelled "a note synced before the `Identity` field existed" as exactly that impossible
    note, and proved two false things at once: `updateNoteFields` merges over the fields a note
    ALREADY has, so writing the missing one was dropped silently while the modification count
    still moved.

    **There WAS a check, and it was one-sided.** `checkFields` rejects a field name the note type
    does not declare and says nothing about a name the type DOES declare that the caller omitted.
    A check that can be one-sided is a check separable from the value it guards — which is the
    argument for the type rather than for a better check.

    **And the field-ORDER rule is a comment repeated three times.** Anki's `modelFieldAdd`
    appends, so a field declared anywhere but last leaves a repaired collection permanently
    reporting a difference it can never fix. That reasoning is written out at `CardSpec.fields`'
    concept-descriptor arm and twice more in `Marker.FieldOrder` — three copies of a rule nothing
    enforces, which is what a missing type looks like from outside.

    **THE SHAPE OF THE FIX, for this part.** A field set constructible only from a
    `NoteTypeSpec`: the spec supplies the names and their order, the caller supplies values by
    name, anything absent is empty rather than missing. `checkFields` is then DELETED rather than
    made symmetric, because the state it looks for stops existing. Gone with it: a missing field,
    an extra field, a wrong order, a misspelled name at construction. NOT gone: a wrong value —
    worth saying, so the type is not later blamed for something it never claimed.

    **WHY THE ASYMMETRY EXISTS AT ALL**, which is the question underneath all four parts. This
    project already applies boundary discipline once: `content/Content.scala` is a closed algebra
    that exists precisely because Laika's types are open and foreign, so the parse boundary is
    where foreign shapes stop. The same reasoning was never applied to AnkiConnect, whose wire
    format is JSON with string keys — and that shape was carried inward instead of being parsed
    at the edge. Not a principle this repository lacks; a principle it applied on one side.

    **Where the full diagnosis lives, and why that is not good enough.** `docs/design/PIPELINE-DESIGN.md`
    surveys every site, and its back-end fact table was independently verified — nine of eleven
    rows opened and all nine accurate. But that document opens with a warning telling readers not
    to implement from it, because its RECOMMENDATION failed adversarial review. **A live problem
    parked inside a discredited document is close to not being recorded at all**, which is why it
    is restated here.

    **Not urgent, and say why:** a note type is not part of the key, so unlike identity work this
    costs the same whenever it is done. It does not compete with the now-or-never column.
title: The Anki-facing seam is stringly typed

description:
**OBSERVATION.** `BuildFailure.shelters` in `plan/VaultScan.scala:305` answers "which of this
author's Anki cards must NOT be inferred deleted" as a method ON THE FAILURE RECORD. So the
protection exists only if a failure record exists. A decision to stop REPORTING something is
therefore, silently and unavoidably, a decision to stop PROTECTING against it.

**THE TWO QUESTIONS ARE NOT THE SAME QUESTION.** "What should we tell the author?" is a judgement
about usefulness and noise. "What must we not conclude about their cards?" is a safety judgement.
They have different reasons and can legitimately differ. Fusing them means the first silently
answers the second.

**THIS IS NOT HYPOTHETICAL — it happened on 2026-09-03.** Marc ruled that an indented, UNMARKED
heading should stop being reported, on the correct ground that both parsers agree about it and
nothing is wrong. Making `UnreadHeadings.failure` return `None` for that case also removed
`OrphanShelter.WholeNote` for it, because the shelter rode on the failure. The outcome happens to
be right — an unmarked heading never produced a card, so there is nothing to protect — but it was
arrived at as a SIDE EFFECT rather than chosen. The agent caught it by reading carefully. The
compiler could not help: there was no case to be non-exhaustive about, no record, no signal.

**WHY THE COUPLING EXISTS, and it is not careless.** The docstring at `VaultScan.scala:293-298`
records the bug it fixed: three consumers each asked their own version of "does this exclude a key
or a note?", so a new failure case had to be remembered in three places and forgetting any of them
compiled clean. Consolidating them means `-Wconf:msg=exhaustive:e` forces every new case to answer
all three at once. That is a real improvement and must not be lost by any fix.

**THE STAKES, from the same docstring.** "An orphan is TAGGED AND SUSPENDED — a live card with
real review history silently out of the review queue. It has happened once already: `Extractor`
records that one image pasted into one table cell flagged fifteen live cards."

**RELATED, AND THE REASON THIS IS WORTH A SEPARATE ITEM.** The identical defect was fixed one
layer down on the same day. `UnreadHeading.withholdsTheNotesCards` hung a planning decision off an
observation; Marc's objection ("Java OOP slop rather than richly modelled ADTs") led to it being
moved out to the two consumers, which were deliberately kept separate because they withhold
DIFFERENT things for reasons that only look alike. `shelters` is the same shape, one level up:
a policy hanging off a report.

---

**SUGGESTIONS, not a choice. Each preserves the exhaustivity guarantee the coupling was built for.**

- Derive the shelter from the OBSERVATION rather than from the report — e.g. the thing that
  detects an unreadable heading yields a protection claim and, separately, an optional report.
  The compiler still forces a total answer, but over the observations rather than over the
  messages.
- Keep `shelters` where it is, and make "report this" a separate field on the failure rather than
  the failure's existence. A failure that is protected-but-silent becomes representable, which it
  currently is not.
- Accept the coupling and require every future narrowing to state explicitly what it does to the
  shelter, as this one did.

**CAUTION.** This is the code path that suspends live cards, and it has already caused one
incident. It should not be untangled while attached to another task.
title: What the tool protects is decided by what it chooses to report

close_reason: Shipped 2026-08-29. model/BlockAnchor.scala with validation and case folding; CardPath gained a fourth case; the identity encodes as src::{id}::/b/{anchor} using the extension point the codec had reserved, so no existing identity moved.
description: A card scoped to a block needs an identity, and a block has nothing intrinsic to offer: position moves when something is inserted above it, and text changes for the very edits a card is about. Every derived candidate failed. The answer is a surrogate, which is the textbook one - and what made it look impossible is that a surrogate must be written down while this tool never writes to the vault. Marc: it does not have to. The author writes the anchor and a cloze block without one is refused.
design:
THE REASONING, MOVED HERE FROM docs/design/CLOZE-REDESIGN.md ON 2026-08-30 AND CUT FROM IT. The document holds the current design; a decision's argument — including the alternatives rejected on the way to it — belongs to the decision. ### Obsidian block references (`^blockid`) — ELIMINATED 2026-08-27, ADOPTED 2026-08-29 > **THIS SECTION ELIMINATED THE MECHANISM THAT IS NOW THE ANSWER**, and how that happened is worth > more than the conclusion was. > > **The first finding was a DEFECT MISTAKEN FOR A PROPERTY.** "A block id prints on the card face" > was true, and it was a bug in this tool rather than a fact about `^blockid`: nothing in the > parser had a production for it, so it fell through as prose. Marc's ruling, 2026-08-29 — *there > is a grammar of Obsidian and this tool should model it, not paper over the places it did not* — > made the repair a production rather than a string stripped on the way out. A block id now lowers > to nothing at all, so no renderer can print one and the defect is unrepresentable rather than > fixed. > > **The second finding was never about the mechanism.** Callouts failing the strict parse blocks > the note they are in, whatever anchors anyone chooses. Still open: `oas-yom`. > > **What separated them was Marc's question**, asked after this section had been read back to him: > *"I said could we **use** `^blockid` — not should the tool **write** it."* The unstated > assumption was that a surrogate key must be written by whoever needs it, and this tool has never > written to the vault. It does not have to: the **author** writes the anchor, Obsidian generates > one with a keystroke, and a cloze block without one is refused — the same contract a heading > already has, where declaring the marker is how you ask for the card. > > _The reasoning below is kept unedited. It was sound on its evidence; the evidence was > incomplete._ The obvious candidate, and Marc's vault is full of them (`[[Modern Mathematics#^Z4YC85FV]]`, with `obsidian-copy-block-link` installed). Obsidian generates them, they survive edits to the block, and they are not prose — everything an anchor should be. **VERIFIED BY EXECUTION, and it kills them:** run through this project's own parser, `The outermost layer is the ==epidermis==. ^abc123` renders as `

The outermost layer is the {{c1::epidermis}}. ^abc123

`. **A block id prints on the card face.** It is card *content*, not metadata. `^` is a delimiter nowhere in the stack — not in Laika's `Markdown.spanParsers`, not in `GitHubFlavor`, not among the six parsers `ObsidianSyntax.bundle` registers — and `Html.escape` covers `& < > " { }` and leaves it alone. A second finding, also VERIFIED, would have blocked them anyway: **every one of the 125 block-id definitions in `References/Modern Mathematics.md` sits inside an Obsidian callout, and callouts fail this tool's strict parse** — `> [!note] Page 31` yields `unresolved link id reference: !note`, because CommonMark reads `[!note]` as a shortcut reference link. It is silent today only because that note has no frontmatter `id`; giving it one, which is exactly what somebody does when they want its annotations to become cards, is what makes the failure appear. _The first finding is **fixed** — `parser/ObsidianSyntax.scala` carries the production and `content/Lower.scala` drops the node. The second is **open** as `oas-yom`. Both were open items 20 and 21 in the markdown tracker that beads replaced on 2026-08-30; the archive at `docs/history/IN-FLIGHT.md` holds their original wording and is not where to look for their status._ ### A plain content hash — ELIMINATED, and instructively Hashing a paragraph and using the digest as its name fails for a reason worth stating, because it generalises: **a cryptographic hash is designed to do the opposite of what an anchor needs.** Avalanche is the point — flip one bit of input, every output bit changes. So fixing a typo re-keys the card. Git blob SHAs fail identically, and per-file besides. ### A. The cloze label as the anchor `==2|epidermis==` — the `2` is author-supplied, note-scoped, and **survives rewriting `epidermis`**, rewording the sentence around it, and reflowing the paragraph. It is precisely the author-typed anchor the `%%card%%` proposal wanted to invent, except it already exists in the syntax and is already used. It also sidesteps that proposal's objection: a duplicated paragraph carries a duplicated **label**, which is note-scoped and which the tool can refuse by name. **And it can dissolve the ordinal-drift defect rather than guard against it.** Today one section is one Anki note with N cards, and a card's ordinal is its cloze number — so inserting a highlight earlier renumbers the later ones and review history re-attaches to different content (`EVOLVABILITY.md` §3.2, still open). If each label-group becomes **its own Anki note with one card**, there are no ordinals to rotate. The defect stops being something to guard and becomes unrepresentable. ~~**A generalisation worth keeping even if the rest is dropped:** do not hash the content — project it onto the part that is already stable. In a cloze block that part is the labels. A key of `(frontmatter id, heading path, the labels in this block)` is content-derived, needs no new syntax, and moves only when the author deliberately renumbers.~~ **WITHDRAWN 2026-08-29. IT ASSUMES LABELS ARE UNIQUE ACROSS A NOTE, AND THEY ARE NOT.** Marc caught this by reading the syntax rather than the prose. A label is scoped to the section it appears in — which is what `extract/Cloze.scala`'s `number` actually does, computing over one section's highlights — so two blocks may each use `1` and `2` meaning different things: ```markdown # Header The ==<<1|radius>>== and the ==<<2|ulna>>== are forearm bones. The ==<<1|femur>>== and the ==<<2|tibia>>== are leg bones. ``` Both project to `(note id, "Header", [1,2])`. **Same key, two different paragraphs.** The projection cannot identify a block, because a label only means something INSIDE a scope and the scope is the thing being named. It is circular. **A SECOND DEFECT, FOUND BEFORE THE FIRST ONE KILLED IT**, recorded so the idea is not revived in a patched form: the label SET is not stable under ADDITION either. Adding a third gap to a paragraph turns `[1,2]` into `[1,2,3]`, re-keying the note and orphaning the cards already in it — a cost paid for an edit that only adds. **It could be made to work by making labels note-scoped**, unique across a whole file. That is a real tax — in a ten-paragraph note the author numbers into the twenties and must remember which numbers are spent — and it is not needed, for the reason the next section gives. **The fork it forces.** If a paragraph holds three groups, do they become one Anki note with three cards, or three notes with one card each? | | one note per block | one note per label-group | | --- | --- | --- | | ordinal drift | still possible for **unlabelled** groups | **unrepresentable** | | anchor needed for the block | **yes — unsolved** | **no** — the label is the anchor | | Anki sibling burying | kept | **lost** | | paragraph text | stored once | duplicated per note | The second makes the anchor problem disappear rather than solving it. **Its only real cost is sibling burying** — Anki's ability to keep two gaps from one paragraph off the same day — and that is the open question for Marc: is seeing them together fine? --- RECOVERED FROM `model/BlockAnchor.scala`'S DOCSTRING ON 2026-08-31, WHEN THAT DOCSTRING WAS CUT. An adversarial review of the cut identified what in it had no home anywhere else. Text marked RECOVERED is the deleted wording; text marked ADDED 2026-08-31 is reasoning written on the day of the restoration and was NOT part of the 2026-08-29 deliberation. ### A similarity fingerprint — ELIMINATED RECOVERED. The eliminated candidates were "a content hash, **a similarity fingerprint**, and a key projected onto the labels inside the block", and every one of them failed "because a name that must be DERIVED from something unstable is unstable". That single generalisation is the argument the deleted text actually made, and it also survives at `docs/design/CLOZE-REDESIGN.md`. Only the fingerprint had gone missing from the repository entirely — the bead's rejected-alternatives section covers the plain hash and the label projection at length, and names neither it nor this generalisation. ADDED 2026-08-31, and not part of the original deliberation. The fingerprint deserves its own line rather than being folded into the hash, because the argument that kills the hash — *avalanche is the point* — invites the rebuttal *then use a digest that does not avalanche*, and a locality-sensitive fingerprint is that rebuttal. It fails for a different reason: it makes identity a matter of degree, so two blocks either side of a threshold are the same card or not depending on a number nobody can justify. Whether the 2026-08-29 discussion reached that reasoning is not recorded anywhere; the standing rule **similarity never decides** forecloses it either way, though that rule is stated about RECOVERY rather than about naming. ### Why the identity side is the one that must refuse RECOVERED. `BlockAnchor` pins the anchor character set as well as the parser, and if the two ever drift, the model is the one that must refuse, because **an identity is forever, and a parse is only until the next run.** ADDED 2026-08-31: a parse that admits too much is corrected by fixing the parser and re-running; an identity that admits too much is already written into somebody's collection, attached to review history, and cannot be withdrawn.

description:
27. ⚠️ **A `#` HEADING ON THE LINE DIRECTLY AFTER A LIST LINE IS SWALLOWED BY THE LIST, AND
    EVERY CONSEQUENCE OF THAT IS SILENT.**

    **How it was found.** Marc opened an Anki card of note type `Obsidian Cloze Sequence`
    (note `1787823966254`, key `essential numbers/scale`) and found it holding five items
    belonging to a different heading, plus the literal text `5 Questions #flashcard/sequence`
    as a list item. Source: `System Design Interview Framework.md`, line 21.

    **The trigger is one missing blank line.**

    ```markdown
    - data size
    # 5 Questions #flashcard/sequence
    ```

    **The mechanism, every link read.** laika-core 1.3.2 follows original Markdown plus the
    PHP Markdown suite and explicitly NOT the CommonMark suite — the same divergence
    `extract/ListIndent.scala` already documents for indentation. It keeps the list open and
    absorbs the `#` line into the item, parsing it there as a nested `ast.Header`. Laika's
    `SectionBuilder` lifts only TOP-LEVEL headers into `Section`s, so it never becomes one.
    `Extractor.walk` matches on `Section`, so the marker is never seen. And
    `content/Lower.scala`'s `case ast.Header` arm — commented "a heading NESTED inside a
    blockquote or a list item … it flattens rather than refusing" — turns it into a
    `Block.Paragraph`, which is how the marker text reaches the card as content.

    **THREE OUTCOMES, MEASURED BY A/B** on copies of one file differing by ONE BLANK LINE.
    Every one of them reports `failures: 0`, `scan: complete`, and exits 0:

    | shape | result |
    |---|---|
    | the swallowed heading carries the marker | its card is never created |
    | a marked heading sits below it, inside the list | no card at all — `notes: 0` |
    | a marked heading sits below it, outside the list | the card is built UNDER THE WRONG PARENT |

    The third is the expensive one. `# Alpha` / list / `# Beta` / `## Gamma #flashcard/1way`
    keys as `alpha / gamma` without the blank line and `beta / gamma` with it. Nothing fails
    to build — the card is well-formed and merely mis-keyed — so **no refusal can reach it**:
    a refusal fires on a `BuildFailure`, and there is none. The heading path is half the card
    identity, so adding the blank line LATER, or letting `conform.nvim`'s prettier add it
    (item 13), re-keys the card: the old note is orphaned and suspended and a replacement is
    created with no review history.

    **BOUNDED, so the gap is not overstated.** A heading immediately after a PARAGRAPH parses
    correctly — Laika's `headerOrParagraph` handles it — and so does one after another heading
    or after a fence. It is specifically heading-after-LIST-ITEM. A sweep of Marc's vault on
    2026-08-27 found ten headings with no blank line above them and exactly ONE after a list
    line: the instance above.

    **WHY THE ONE GUARD BUILT FOR THIS CLASS MISSED IT.** `extract/ListIndent.scala` exists to
    report "this tool's parser reads this list differently from Obsidian, so the card would say
    something the note does not". Its own scanner matches `^#{1,6}(\s|$)` and, on a match, does
    `heading = lineNumber; open = List.empty` — "A heading closes every open list." **So the
    scanner believes the line is a heading and closes the list, while Laika keeps the list open
    and swallows it.** The disagreement is present inside the very file whose job is to report
    disagreements, and goes unreported because the only thing compared afterwards is
    INDENTATION. A scope note naming this was added to that docstring on 2026-08-27.

    **The vault side is a one-character fix and it is Marc's to make**, and it is not free:
    `essential numbers/motivation ?` re-keys to `5 questions/motivation ?`, so the run reports
    one orphan and one create beside the update and the new `5 questions` card. Measured
    read-only against the live collection the same day: every affected card is at 0 reps, so
    no review history is at stake in THIS instance.

description:
**OBSERVATION.** `extract/Extractor.scala` computes "what a concept-descriptor card's concept is"
twice, from the same inputs, with the same expression, for two different consumers:

    74:    val concept = ancestorTitles.lastOption.getOrElse(fileName)
    762:          val concept = ancestorTitles.lastOption.getOrElse(fileName)

Line 74 is inside `recallFromLocation(marker, title, ancestorTitles, fileName)`, which builds the
`RecallText` used for deck clamping. Line 762 is on the extraction path and feeds the card's
`Concept` FIELD.

**THEY ARE REQUIRED TO AGREE, and the code says so.** The comment immediately below line 762
reads: "The last ancestor is bound one line above as the Concept, which Card 1 of this note type
asks the reviewer to RECALL. Printing it in the breadcrumb would print the answer." So the recall
text and the field are two views of one fact by design.

**Nothing enforces it.** Change the fallback in one — to the parent folder, say, or to the note's
frontmatter title — and the deck clamp and the card's own field disagree silently. No test would
notice: each consumer is correct with respect to its own copy.

**HOW IT WAS FOUND, 2026-09-04.** Nobody was looking for it. Three agents debating move detection
(`oas-ugc`) disputed a line-number citation: one cited `:74` for the concept, another pointed out
that line is inside a different function and the intended line is `:762`. Both are true, and
checking which was right is what exposed that the derivation exists twice. Verified independently
from the main session.

**WHY IT IS PRIORITY 3 RATHER THAN HIGHER.** The two copies agree today, so nothing is wrong in
the collection. This is a latent divergence, not an active defect — the same shape as the
"contracts held where nothing checks them" class (`oas-5x6`), one file inward.

---

**SUGGESTIONS, not a choice.**

- Have the extraction path call `recallFromLocation`'s derivation rather than restate it, so the
  rule has one home.
- Or extract the one line into a named function both call, which is the smaller change and makes
  the shared rule greppable.
- Or leave both and add a test asserting they agree for a representative set of inputs — weakest,
  since it pins agreement rather than removing the possibility of disagreement.

**RELATED.** `oas-jsm` (a table with a blank first header cell) came out of the same debate and is
also an extraction-level defect that move detection merely exposed. `oas-ugc` records the debate
and the design it produced.
title: What a card's concept is, is derived in two places with nothing holding them in agreement

RULED BY MARC, 2026-09-01: "the ID, the template, shall be part of our 'package' (it is a part of
our system, requirements)".

WHAT IS MISSING. Every card's identity derives from the note's frontmatter `id`. The tool requires
one — `README.md:124`: "A file produces cards only if its frontmatter carries an `id`" — and ships
no way to get one. `randomUUID` appears nowhere in this repository. The README never says where an
id comes from.

The only thing that produces them is one file in Marc's own vault,
`Templates/Card note.md`, holding `id: <% crypto.randomUUID() %>` — an Obsidian Templater template.
Measured 2026-09-01: 24 of the vault's 25 ids are lowercase hex UUIDs; the 25th is the template
itself. So the template is the mechanism, not a coincidence of how Marc happens to write.

WHY IT BELONGS IN THE PACKAGE. The tool already treats the Anki half of this as its own
responsibility: it owns five note types and installs them with `install-note-types`, on the ruling
that it must never write to a note type it did not create. The vault half has the same shape — a
requirement the tool imposes, that the tool should therefore supply — and it does not.

A new user today reads that an `id` is required and has to invent the mechanism. Whatever they
invent decides whether identities survive case-folding, whether they collide, and whether the
`FrontmatterId` type's assumptions hold.

WHAT THIS WOULD MEAN, not settled here:
  - The template ships in `resources/`, beside the note types.
  - Something installs it. `install-note-types` has the shape to copy from; the target is the
    vault's own template folder, which is a WRITE TO THE VAULT — legitimate under the 2026-09-01
    ruling that not writing is a default with justified exceptions, and this is exactly the kind
    of exception that ruling contemplated. Worth deciding whether it is an install step, a
    documented snippet the author pastes, or both.
  - It depends on the Templater plugin, which is a dependency the tool does not currently declare.
    `README.md`'s requirements list names Anki, AnkiConnect and a JVM, not this.
  - The lowercase-hex property stops being an observation about Marc's vault and becomes something
    the package guarantees — which retires the open item about whether the case-folding hazard is
    inert.

ONE THING FOUND WHILE MEASURING, worth checking separately: the template file itself is scanned by
the tool, and its `id` is the literal string `<% crypto.randomUUID() %>`. Nobody has looked at what
that produces — a card, a refusal, or a confusing failure.

description:
When a card's identity moves — a heading reworded, an unlabelled cloze phrase edited — the Anki
card is tagged orphaned:: and suspended. Its review history is intact. What is missing is the
RECONNECTION: nothing offers to bind the orphan to the card that replaced it.

BUILT ALREADY: tiers 1 and 2, which recover a note whose identity tag is unreadable by matching an
exact content hash, then exact fields. They work only while the content is unchanged.

THIS IS THE NEXT TIER: rank candidates by SIMILAR content when the exact match fails.

THE CONSTRAINT THAT MAKES IT SAFE, already written at Planner.identityErrorFor: a suggestion may
only ever NAME a candidate. A wrong rebind moves review history onto the wrong card, silently and
irreversibly. This project's standing rule is that fuzzy matching may RANK but never APPLY, and
this is the sanctioned half of it.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN IT DID: the cloze design now leans on it. Marc's framing, 2026-08-29 —
a card whose key moves is not destroyed, it is disconnected and recoverable, and the word
"fragile" that the conversation kept using was wrong. That reframing is what dissolved the choice
between per-group packaging and note-scoped labels. It is only true once this exists.

## Identity is a matching problem, not a naming problem

_Raised by Claude 2026-08-27, answering Marc's request for a deeper reflection._

**SETTLED 2026-08-29, AND NOT THE WAY THIS SECTION PROPOSES.** Identity stays a PURE FUNCTION OF
THE VAULT — derived, deterministic, the same notes always producing the same cards whatever the
collection happens to hold. What this section proposes would make identity depend on Anki's current
state, so two runs over one vault could diverge. That property was never weighed when the section
was written, and it is worth more than what matching was going to buy.

**WHAT SURVIVES OF IT, AND IT IS THE USEFUL HALF.** Comparing old text with new is exactly right as
a way to RANK candidates for a human to approve — which is this project's standing rule about fuzzy
matching, and which is already designed as recovery tier 3 (oas-4ti, and the long
comment at `plan/Planner.scala`'s `identityErrorFor`). It belongs there, on the suggest side of the
line, and not in the identity function. See *How per-paragraph is actually unblocked* below.

Both candidates below assume identity means a **name** — a label, a block id, a fingerprint;
something written down that must survive arbitrary editing on its own. That may be answering a
harder question than the tool actually asks.

**The tool does not need to name a card. It needs to pair the cards Anki holds with the cards the
vault now produces.** Those are different problems:

- **Naming** is global and one-sided. The name must survive unaided, with nothing to compare against.
- **Matching** is local and two-sided. Both collections are in hand at the moment of the sync.

Matching also runs in a tiny arena: the scope is a single note — typically one to ten cards — and
**Anki's `Text` field holds the previous content verbatim**, so the old text itself is available for
comparison, not merely a hash of it.

### The drift case dissolves with no fuzziness at all

Ordinal drift is the failure this document exists to prevent: insert a highlight earlier in a
paragraph and every later ordinal rotates, so review history silently re-attaches to different
content under an ordinary update.

```
old note in Anki:  {{c1::radius}}   {{c2::ulna}}
new text in vault: {{c1::forearm}}  {{c2::radius}}  {{c3::ulna}}
```

**Exact string equality pairs old `c1` with new `c2`, and old `c2` with new `c3`.** No threshold,
no similarity score, no git history, no author-supplied label. The failure this whole document is
organised around is resolved by comparing strings.

### What is left over, and where it goes

The residue is a card whose text was **edited and moved in the same sitting**, leaving exact
matching no partner for it. In a scope of five cards that is one or two items — and it is precisely
the shape `REVIEW-QUEUE.md` describes: propose the pairing, show what it costs, let the author
confirm.

That also honours the standing ruling that **fuzzy matching may rank but must never apply on its
own.** The ranking becomes a proposal in a queue, not a silent write.

### What it would change about labels

Labels stop being a requirement and become **a way to buy certainty on the residue** — written
where you want a card pinned, not on every highlight. That is a materially different burden to ask
an author to carry, and it is the strongest argument against treating candidate A as the default.

### What has not been checked, and must be before this is relied on

- **That AnkiConnect returns the `Text` field for cloze notes on `notesInfo`.** Assumed here,
  UNVERIFIED, and the entire reframe rests on it.
- **What matching does when a card is genuinely deleted** rather than moved. Two leftovers must not
  be paired with each other merely because both were left over — that would silently graft one
  card's history onto unrelated content, which is the exact harm being prevented.
- **Whether within-note matching is enough**, or whether a card can move between notes and needs a
  wider arena.

### B. A similarity fingerprint, traced across git commits

Marc's, and it corrects a claim made against it in conversation. The objection was that a
similarity fingerprint cannot be an identifier because similarity needs a threshold, and a
threshold is a number nobody can justify — the same grounds on which `EVOLVABILITY.md` rejected a
proportional orphan guard.

**That objection holds for a single comparison and fails for a traced one.** Comparing two
arbitrary states six months apart is hard. Comparing **consecutive commits** is easy, and chaining
small deltas crosses the six months without ever making a large comparison. This is exactly how
`git log --follow` tracks a file across renames, and it works.

It also answers the threshold objection rather than dodging it: git ships a similarity threshold
(`-M`, 50% by default) that has been exercised on every repository in the world for twenty years.
Inheriting a battle-tested default is categorically different from inventing a number.

**Keep the two mechanisms separate**, because they have different properties:

- **The fingerprint is the key** — a pure function of current content, derivable from the vault
  alone with no memory. That preserves the property the design rests on: a sidecar is a cache,
  never an oracle (`CARD-MODEL.md`).
- **Git is the rename detector** — consulted only to *migrate a binding* whose key has moved:
  *"Anki holds key A, the vault now has key B, and here is the commit where A became B."*

Kept separate, identity never becomes a function of history — which would be the expensive change.
History is evidence for a **repair**, and the design already has a shape for that: `relink`, the
manual version, reattaching an orphan to a new key. Git-as-evidence is the same operation with the
pairing **supplied rather than guessed**, which satisfies the standing ruling that anything fuzzy
may rank but never apply. Git is not guessing; it is reading a record of the edit.

**Degradation is graceful, which is rare and worth having.** No commits means no trace, which means
today's behaviour — orphan plus create. The tool is strictly better when git is used and no worse
when it is not. As Marc put it: one should not fight indiscipline.

description:
38. **CONTRACTS THIS REPOSITORY OWNS ARE HELD IN PLACES IT CANNOT SEE, AND NOTHING CHECKS THEM.**
    Found by Marc asking, twice, whether anything else depended on the identity tag. **Nothing
    here could have answered.** Partly fixed; the class is not.

    **INSTANCE ONE — FIVE CONSUMERS OF ONE FORMAT, ONE OUTSIDE THE REPOSITORY.** A card's
    identity was written by the planner, decoded by `locate`, found by the add-on's
    `source_tag`, CONSTRUCTED by the add-on's drill search (`tag:src::<id>::*`), and
    CONSTRUCTED AGAIN in a `curl` one-liner in Marc's Obsidian configuration. `README.md`
    presented that last one as the feature's whole trick — *composable without asking this tool
    anything, so the binding costs nothing.* What it bought was a copy of the identity format in
    a file this repository cannot read, test or migrate.

    **TWO OF THE FOUR BREAKAGES WOULD HAVE BEEN SILENT**, which is why this is a defect class
    rather than an inconvenience. Pressing `e` and the Anki drill menu do nothing visible. The
    Obsidian-to-Anki browse keystroke opens an EMPTY BROWSE WINDOW and a drill builds an EMPTY
    DECK — which read as *this note made no cards* and *nothing to drill*. Plausible wrong
    answers, which is the failure this project is built against.

    **FIXED for this instance**: a `browse` subcommand now owns the search, so the keystroke
    passes a note id and knows nothing else; the add-on reads the field; the drill search asks
    for both homes. `model/CardSearch.test.scala` holds the test that was missing — it asserts
    the search this tool hands out MATCHES THE IDENTITY THIS TOOL WRITES, and fails if either
    side moves alone.

    **INSTANCE TWO — 37 TESTS THAT NOTHING RAN.** `addon/obsidian_edit/core_test.py` covered the
    Python half of the edit workflow, including the exact function that would break, and `just
    test` ran the Scala suite alone. There is no CI. A test file nobody runs is worse than none,
    because its existence reads as coverage. **FIXED**: `just test` now depends on `addon-test`.

    **INSTANCE THREE — SIX OBSIDIAN COMMANDS, TWO DOCUMENTED.** `README.md`'s binding table names
    two; Marc's `.obsidian/plugins/obsidian-shellcommands/data.json` holds six Anki ones. Nothing
    generates them, nothing reads them, nothing compares them. **The symptom that surfaced it**:
    his `install-note-types` command was frozen without `--repair`, a flag added after he wrote
    it, so a note-type repair was unavailable from the tool he actually uses. **NOT FIXED.**

    **WHAT WOULD ACTUALLY CLOSE IT, in order of value.**

    1. **Make the outside hold nothing volatile.** A shell command should pass a note id and
       call the binary — never build a search, never speak AnkiConnect's protocol, never quote
       JSON. Done for browse; the drill already did it by calling a custom add-on action.
    2. **Generate what must live outside**, using the pattern already proven for note types:
       report what differs, repair only when asked, never touch what the tool did not create.
       The plugin keeps its commands in a JSON file that can be read and written. **CONSTRAINT
       FOUND 2026-08-29**: Obsidian holds that file in memory, so a write while it runs is
       silently overwritten by its own copy on the next settings save. Generation is therefore
       "write it, then restart Obsidian" — a ceremony, which argues for it being rare, which it
       becomes exactly when the commands stop holding volatile knowledge.
    3. **A `doctor` command** for what generation cannot cover: is the add-on installed, is it
       the version this repository holds, are the note types current.

    **WHY IT WAS INVISIBLE, which is the part to keep.** Nothing tests a seam. Each side was
    tested against its own idea of the contract — the Scala wrote tags and tested that; the
    Python read tags and tested that — and no test asserted the two agreed. The golden record is
    EXTRACT-LEVEL, built from the vault walk, so it pins the identity this tool DERIVES and would
    not have noticed the tag ceasing to be written. Five consumers accumulated against an
    unguarded format while every suite stayed green.
title: Contracts this repository owns are held where nothing checks them

WHAT THE FAMILY IS. Places where this tool's markdown parser and Obsidian's read the same file
differently. The document's counter-argument for building it has since come true twice: the family
gained a member every time anybody looked, and a silent member cost a card. `oas-30t` (P1) is that
member — a `#` heading on the line directly after a list line is swallowed by the list, and Marc
found an Anki card holding five items belonging to a different heading plus the literal text
`5 Questions #flashcard/sequence`. The trigger is one missing blank line, and every consequence of
it was silent.

THE SHAPE, AND MARC IS THE ONE WHO FOUND IT. The document lists four "candidates" for where a check
runs — more rules inside the refusal path, a `lint` subcommand, a block inside `inspect`, an
Obsidian plugin — and reads as though one must be chosen. Marc's question: "isn't there a synergy /
re-use possible of the underlying mechanisms / rules?"

There is, and it is already built. `extract/ListIndent.scala` is a pure detector over RAW SOURCE:
`scan(body, bodyFirstLine) -> Report` of `Finding(line, found, needed, text)`, plus
`explain(findings) -> String`. It knows nothing about cards, contacts nothing, and carries its own
test file. `extract/Extractor.scala:223` is merely A CONSUMER — it calls `scan` and turns findings
into a refusal. `model/CardSpec.scala:174` records that the boundary was defended once already,
deliberately refusing to carry `ListIndent.Finding` into `model/`.

So the candidates are not alternatives. They are CONSUMERS OF ONE DETECTION LAYER:

  - THE RULES ARE THE LAYER. `ListIndent` is the first, and has the right shape. New members —
    starting with the swallowed heading — join it as siblings rather than being buried in the
    extractor.
  - REFUSAL STAYS A CONSUMER. Where a disagreement would silently mis-build a card, sync refuses.
  - `lint` IS A SECOND CONSUMER, and the one that matters: it reads a vault, writes nothing,
    contacts no collection, and is therefore wirable to a save hook or a pre-commit hook. That is
    the only surface that speaks at AUTHORING TIME, which the document argues is the consequential
    difference: "it decides whether the author still remembers what they meant."
  - `inspect` could be a third for the cost of a report block. Not required.

THIS INVERTS THE COST ARGUMENT the assistant gave before Marc asked his question. `lint` is not the
expensive option. The detectors are the expensive part, one exists with the right boundary, and
surfaces are cheap once the rules are a layer.

ALREADY DECIDED AND INHERITED, not settled here: report, never repair (repair belongs to a
formatter); and miss rather than over-report, because a false refusal costs more than a missed one.

STILL OPEN, and still Marc's — the document's other two questions:
  - Whether rows 3, 4 and 5 belong in the same check as rows 1 and 2. They are one CLASS (the
    parsers disagree) but rows 1-2 are structure the tool MIS-READS while 4-5 are constructs it
    does not read at all. One check or two.
  - The name. "lint" implies style; this is not style, it is "the two parsers disagree about your
    file". `check` or `conflicts` may age better. Marc's call, and renames are his to run.

WHAT UNBLOCKS. `oas-30t` is P1 and blocked on this decision: widening `ListIndent` closes two of its
three measured outcomes and not the third — the one that re-keys a card and destroys its review
history. That third one needs the check.
title: The parser-disagreement rules become a layer, with refusal and lint as consumers

DOES \begin{align} TYPESET UNDER ANKI'S MATHJAX, or is aligned required? This is the only candidate found so far for translating the TeX BODY rather than its delimiters, and it decides whether 'delimiters only' survives as the shape of the feature.

DOES MATHJAX TYPESET TEX WHOSE BRACES ARRIVED AS CHARACTER REFERENCES? It should — a browser decodes them while parsing the field's HTML, and content/AsHtml.scala already argues the emitted field post-decoding is character-for-character what pass-through would have produced. AsHtml leaves the same question open for the same reason.

DOES THE VAULT REACH FOR PACKAGES ANKI DOES NOT LOAD? The Anki half is settled by reading the shipped config: no mhchem, no physics, and textmacros explicitly removed, so \text{} takes a narrower grammar than Obsidian allows. The vault half is a grep.

DOES OBSIDIAN RENDER A MULTI-LINE BLOCK WITH \\ CORRECTLY? If it does, the two parsers disagree and it is a member of the family in PARSER-DISAGREEMENTS. If Obsidian is equally broken, the vault has been carrying broken maths and this is an improvement rather than a repair.

description:
**OBSERVATION.** Both backup mechanisms for this project are correct and neither is triggered by
anything. They run only when a person or an agent invokes them by hand.

**EVIDENCE, 2026-09-03.** The `beads-backup` branch contained exactly ONE publishing commit in its
entire history — `bd backup export-git`, 2026-08-30 23:09 — the day the backup config was written.
Nothing had published since. The live tracker held 91 issues; the published copy held 53.

`bd backup status` reported the mechanism healthy throughout, because it shows the age of the
LOCAL snapshot (which bd refreshes on an interval when bd commands run) rather than the age of the
published one.

**THIS IS THE THIRD SIGHTING OF THE SAME FAILURE.**

  - MAY 2026. `~/beads-recovery-2026-05-29/DOLTHUB-RECOVERY-ISSUE.md` records that during a real
    recovery "pushes had been silently failing, so the remote is behind the corruption point".
  - 30 AUGUST 2026. `.beads/config.yaml` documents the same thing happening and being fixed by
    setting `backup.enabled` explicitly, with a comment naming the failure mode: "nothing was
    broken, a command simply was not running, and the only symptom was a number in a status line
    nobody had read."
  - 3 SEPTEMBER 2026. Found again, by inspection rather than by any alarm.

**WHAT EXISTS AND IS NOT WIRED.** Marc wrote `.mise/tasks/beads/{backup,check}` on 2026-05-29 —
the day of the May incident — with an ALARM sentinel raised on failed push or staleness and
cleared only on success, intended for a status-bar surfacer. `~/.beads/backup-watch/` records four
successful runs, all on 2026-05-29, and none since. The only loaded launchd agent matching `bead*`
on this machine is `com.marc.check-beads-version`, a weekly version check. Nothing invokes the
backup or the checker, so the alarm cannot fire. (Established with the web-app session, which
found the same shape independently in its own project.)

**A CONSTRAINT ON ANY FIX.** `bd backup init` FAILS in bd 0.62.0 with "no store available" while
every other bd command works. The Dolt-native backup taken on 2026-09-03 had to be made by calling
`DOLT_BACKUP('sync-url', …)` directly against the running server. So an automated Dolt-native
backup cannot rely on `bd backup init` / `bd backup sync` in this version.

---

**WHAT IS IN PLACE AS OF 2026-09-03, both verified rather than assumed:**

  - Issues, off-machine: `beads-backup` branch pushed to GitHub, 91 issues, current.
  - Database with history: `~/beads-backups/yet-another-obsidian-anki-sync`, 2.0 MB, 205 commits.
    VERIFIED BY RESTORING IT into a scratch directory and counting — 91 issues, all present.

Both were made by hand. Neither will refresh on its own. That is exactly the state that produced
the three sightings above.

**SUGGESTIONS, not a choice.** Schedule the publishing step and the Dolt-native backup; wire the
existing alarm sentinel to something that surfaces it; or decide explicitly that backups are
manual and remove the machinery that implies otherwise. The worst option is the current one, where
correct machinery exists and reports success while doing nothing.
title: Beads backups are not scheduled, and have lapsed silently three times

description:
A cloze card scoped to a block is keyed by `(note id, ^blockid)`. The GROUPS inside that block
are keyed separately, and an unlabelled group is keyed by its own text — so editing the text,
even to fix a typo, retires the card.

That is a defensible contract and it is the one the documentation already states. The question
is whether it is the one we want, now that the surrounding pieces have changed.

WHAT CHANGED UNDER IT

- A block now has a stable name of its own, so the NOTE survives an edit even when a group does
  not. Before, both moved together.
- Recovery tier 3 — ranking candidates for a broken identity by similar content — is designed and
  unbuilt. With it, a retired group becomes a proposal to reconnect rather than a loss. Marc's
  framing on 2026-08-29: the honest word is DISCONNECTED AND RECOVERABLE, never "fragile".

THE ALTERNATIVE

Require a label on every cloze highlight. Then nothing is ever retired by an edit. Rejected in
conversation as "a heading by another name" — ceremony that defeats the point of highlighting a
phrase anywhere and getting a card.

WHY IT IS NOT MERELY ACADEMIC

The documentation claims editing the text produces an orphan, visible in the prune list. It
demonstrably does not: the planner has no cloze awareness at all, so no orphan is ever produced
for a retired group. Whatever is decided here, that claim has to stop being made.
title: Decide what an unlabelled cloze highlight is keyed by

rather than hypothetical: `^` identifies the block, and a label lives inside the highlight as
`==<<N|text>>==`. Anyone reopening the label syntax needs to know `^` is spoken for twice over.

## The marker: what syntax says "this is a cloze"

_OPEN, raised by Marc 2026-08-27 and NOT settled. It sits upstream of everything below, because it
decides which text in a note the tool looks at in the first place._

The tool reads `==highlighted==`, Obsidian's own highlight syntax, chosen for two stated reasons:
it renders as a highlight, which is apt for "phrase you will be asked about", and it is the
convention across the Obsidian spaced-repetition ecosystem.

Adopting it **fully** — every `==…==` anywhere is a cloze, no heading marker, no declaration — is
the shortest route to what Marc asked for: *highlight a phrase anywhere and get a card.* The price
is that `==` becomes **reserved**, unavailable as a third level of emphasis beside bold and italic.
Marc has said he is willing to pay it.

### The three options, and what separates them

| written as | renders in Obsidian as | leaves `==` free for emphasis | can you see which highlights are cards |
|---|---|---|---|
| `==radius==` | a highlight | no | **no** |
| `<<radius>>` | the literal text `<<radius>>` | yes | yes |
| `==<<radius>>==` | a highlight reading `<<radius>>` | yes | yes |

**The hybrid is Marc's proposal, and its strength is how it fails.** A bare custom delimiter
renders as literal brackets and no highlight at all — on mobile, in a preview, on a machine without
the plugin. The hybrid still gets a real Obsidian highlight in every one of those places; it merely
has visible brackets inside it.

### What CSS can and cannot do

**CSS alone cannot hide the inner `<<>>`.** Obsidian renders `==<<radius>>==` as
`<mark><<radius>></mark>` — HTML identical to a plain highlight, with the brackets a fragment of a
text node. CSS selects elements, and there is no element here to select. This is the same wall the
`1|` group labels hit, for the same reason.

**A plugin can, and gets more for the same work.** Post-process each `<mark>` whose text matches
`<<…>>`: strip the brackets, add a class. Clozes then carry their own colour, visibly distinct from
emphasis highlights. This is the plugin possibility already noted for hiding the group labels — not
a second one.

### What the decision turns on

If `==` is not wanted for emphasis, the hybrid's one remaining benefit is that **you can tell at a
glance which highlights are cards.** The plain form gives no way to know without checking. So the
question is narrow: is that worth four extra characters on every cloze ever written?

~~**Nobody has decided.**~~ **DECIDED BY MARC 2026-08-28, AND BUILT THE SAME DAY.** The hybrid
won: a cloze is `==<<text>>==`, and a bare `==highlight==` is an ordinary Obsidian highlight that
makes no card. Four characters buy the property reserving `==` could not — you can see, by looking
at a note, which of its highlights are cards.

**The migration cost nothing, which is the strongest fact about it.** The fixture vault's cloze
notes were rewritten to the new spelling and the golden record of every card that vault produces
came out BYTE-IDENTICAL: not one card identity and not one field value moved. That is not luck. An
unlabelled deletion is keyed by its own text, and stripping the brackets leaves the text alone — so
this changed a syntax and not a collection.

**What it also bought, unplanned:** finding clozes WITHOUT a heading marker became safe. Before it,
scanning every block for highlights would have swept up every emphasis highlight in the vault. Now
only `<<…>>` counts, so "find every cloze in this note" is exact rather than a guess. That was a
prerequisite for everything below, and it is done.

**A plugin can, and gets more for the same work.** Post-process each `<mark>` whose text matches
`<<…>>`: strip the brackets, add a class. Clozes then carry their own colour, visibly distinct from
emphasis highlights. This is the plugin possibility already noted for hiding the group labels — not
a second one.

### What the decision turns on

If `==` is not wanted for emphasis, the hybrid's one remaining benefit is that **you can tell at a
glance which highlights are cards.** The plain form gives no way to know without checking. So the
question is narrow: is that worth four extra characters on every cloze ever written?

~~**Nobody has decided.**~~ **DECIDED BY MARC 2026-08-28, AND BUILT THE SAME DAY.** The hybrid
won: a cloze is `==<<text>>==`, and a bare `==highlight==` is an ordinary Obsidian highlight that
makes no card. Four characters buy the property reserving `==` could not — you can see, by looking
at a note, which of its highlights are cards.

**The migration cost nothing, which is the strongest fact about it.** The fixture vault's cloze
notes were rewritten to the new spelling and the golden record of every card that vault produces
came out BYTE-IDENTICAL: not one card identity and not one field value moved. That is not luck. An
unlabelled deletion is keyed by its own text, and stripping the brackets leaves the text alone — so
this changed a syntax and not a collection.

**What it also bought, unplanned:** finding clozes WITHOUT a heading marker became safe. Before it,
scanning every block for highlights would have swept up every emphasis highlight in the vault. Now
only `<<…>>` counts, so "find every cloze in this note" is exact rather than a guess. That was a
prerequisite for everything below, and it is done.

---
title: A cloze is written ==<<text>>==, and a bare highlight is emphasis

RULED BY MARC, 2026-09-01, and it supersedes the question it was asked in answer to.

An audit found twelve rules across the corpus attributed to Marc with no bead, commit or quotation
behind them. The proposed remedy was to verify each. Marc's answer, on the first one that turned out
genuinely to be his:

  "both mine, but again 'ruled by Marc' does not have its place in the doc. i prefer nuance & hedge
   instead of rigid & cocky over-confidance..."

SO THE REMEDY IS NOT VERIFICATION. IT IS REGISTER. Whether or not a claim is his, a document must
not lean on his authority to carry it. State the reasoning and let it stand or fall; where the
reasoning is incomplete, say so. An appeal to authority is what let twelve unsourced rules read as
settled in the first place, and verifying them one by one would have left the mechanism intact.

WHAT TO DO, EVERYWHERE IN docs/ AND IN CODE COMMENTS:
  - Remove "Ruled by Marc", "Marc's answer", "decided by the author" and the rest as the GROUND of a
    claim. Keep a date and a name only where it is genuinely a decision record — a bead, or a commit
    message — not in prose that a reader will take as settled.
  - Prefer the hedge that is true over the absolute that reads stronger. "This is the default and no
    exception has been argued" beats "this is the central property".
  - Where a rule's justification is thin, the document says it is thin.

26. **A DEFERRED RETYPE IS MODELLED AS AN ABSENT ACTION, NOT AS A STATE THE CARD IS IN.**
    _Recorded 2026-08-27._

    `RetypeVerdict` — `WillApply`, `DeferredByPolicy`, `RefusedByShapes`, `ShapesUnavailable` — is
    a verdict about a PLAN. Every case answers "what will this run do?" and none answers "what is
    true of this card right now?". So the tool can say *I am not doing this* and has no way at all
    to say **"this card is currently asking a different question from the one your vault asks."**

    **What that cost.** The run printed `Leaving them is safe: a note that is not moved simply

    REVIEWS: the card went on asking the wrong question and Marc went on answering it. A reader
    given a reassurance has no reason to look further.

    **The general shape, which is why this is worth recording rather than only fixing.** This
    project keeps finding CONDITIONS THE TOOL CREATES AND HAS NO NAME FOR, and each has been
    solved one at a time without the underlying gap moving:

description:
42. **A COLLECTION CANNOT TELL ONE VAULT'S CARDS FROM ANOTHER'S.** Designed with Marc 2026-08-30,
    replacing a warning the README had carried since the beginning. **Nothing is built.**

    **The hazard.** Nothing this tool writes records which vault a note came from. The reconciler
    enumerates every note carrying an identity in one query — it must, because an orphan is by
    definition a key the markdown does not have, so it can never be found by a lookup driven from
    the markdown. Sync a second vault into the same Anki profile and the first vault's cards are
    absent from the second's markdown, so every one of them is flagged and suspended.

    **THE README PRESENTED THIS AS A RULE TO LIVE BY** — in capitals, with a warning sign, third
    in the document. Marc's response on 2026-08-30: *"I think this is a mistake."* It is a defect
    with a fix, not a constraint users must absorb.

    ### The fix, in three parts

    **1. A `Vault` field beside `Identity`, and it is the discriminator.** Note-level, written only
    by this tool, invisible in the author's tag tree. Adding a field to a note type this tool owns
    is a proven non-migration — done twice in the week of 2026-08-28, with `Reveal` and with
    `Identity`, and the golden record moved by one empty line each time.

    **2. Its value is the vault directory's LEAF NAME, with the absolute path recorded beside it.**
    Marc's first instinct was the absolute path alone, and the consequence decided against it:
    the field answers *does this note belong to the vault being synced*, so an absolute path means
    that **moving or renaming the vault directory makes every note in the collection look foreign
    at once** — one `mv` and the whole collection flags as orphaned. The leaf name survives
    relocation. The absolute path is still worth recording, so a message can say *these notes were
    synced from `/old/path`* without the MATCH depending on it.

    **3. A unique vault name is a contract, enforced.** Two vaults whose directories share a leaf
    name must be refused by name, and the message says the fix: rename one directory. That contract
    is what makes the leaf name usable as an identity in the first place.

    ### The deck path, which is a separate benefit and needs no new mechanism

    Decks should read `Obsidian::<vault name>::…`, derived from the vault rather than typed. Marc
    asked for it for **navigation and legibility** rather than for correctness: without it, a
    second vault's folders interleave with the first's under one root and the tree is unreadable.

    **ALREADY EXPRESSIBLE TODAY.** `--deck-root` splits on `::` (`cli/Cli.scala:205`), so
    `--deck-root "Obsidian::my-vault"` produces exactly that tree now. What is missing is deriving
    the name so it is right by default rather than by the author remembering a flag.

    ### Why the deck must NOT be the discriminator

    Filtering the enumeration by deck is the tempting shortcut and it is wrong, for a reason that
    has nothing to do with user discipline. **Anki's filtered decks RELOCATE cards** — a filtered
    deck sets the card's deck to itself and remembers the original separately — so while one
    exists, every card in it is outside `Obsidian::…` as far as any deck search can tell. A
    deck-filtered enumeration would therefore stop seeing those cards, decide they were deleted,
    and **create duplicates** — and could not move them back, because it could no longer see them.
    The mechanism would depend on the thing it was fixing.

    **MEASURED, NOT IMAGINED.** Exactly this state was found in Marc's own collection on
    2026-08-29: three cards stranded in a leftover `Drill — Function Space` filtered deck, left by
    testing the drill binding. His own drill command creates that state deliberately, every time
    it is used.

    _Marc's objection to the fragility argument was that a user should not move cards in Anki, and
    that is right — but the hazard is Anki itself, not the user. The same shape as `leech` and
    `marked`, which decided the tag namespace in item 9._
design:
RULED BY MARC, 2026-09-01. This supersedes both the "one vault per Anki profile" framing this bead
opened with and the two-value field designed on 2026-08-30.

ONE FIELD, HOLDING THE VAULT'S ABSOLUTE PATH. The leaf of that path is DERIVED wherever it is
needed, never stored beside it: the 2026-08-30 design stored the leaf and recorded the path next to
it, which is one fact written twice and two values that can disagree.

WHAT EACH IS FOR.
  - MATCHING — "is this note mine?" — compares the LEAF of the stored path against the leaf of the
    vault being synced. That is what makes the field survive `mv ~/vault ~/Documents/vault`: the
    path changes, the leaf does not. Matching on the whole path instead would make one move read
    every card in the collection as foreign, flagging and suspending the lot. This is the hazard
    that decided against a bare path on 2026-08-30, and deriving the leaf answers it without
    needing a second field.
  - REPORTING — the stored path is what lets a run say *these notes were synced from `/old/path`*.
  - THE DECK — the leaf becomes a deck level, so a card's deck reads `Obsidian::<vault>::…` and two
    vaults are visibly apart in the deck tree. Derived, like the match.

TWO VAULTS WHOSE PATHS END IN THE SAME LEAF ARE REFUSED, by name, saying which two paths collided.
`~/work/notes` and `~/personal/notes` both derive `notes`, which would merge two vaults into one
deck subtree and make each look like the other's.

WHAT NEITHER DESIGN SURVIVES, stated so nobody re-derives it: RENAMING the vault directory changes
the leaf and breaks the match. Storing both values would not have helped — the leaf is stale either
way. A rename is reconciled by a person here as it is everywhere else in this tool.

DETECTION OVER ENFORCEMENT, WHICH THE ONE-FIELD SHAPE MAKES POSSIBLE. When the leaf matches and the
stored path does not, the tool knows the vault moved and can say so — *these notes were synced from
`/old/path`, you are now syncing from `/new/path`* — rather than silently accepting or silently
refusing. Two stored values could not do this: they would already disagree with each other.

WHAT THIS SUPERSEDES IN THE DOCUMENTS. `docs/reference/REQUIREMENTS.md` filed vault-blindness under
"Constraints on any implementation" as a consequence users absorb; that placement is withdrawn.
`README.md:38` and `:50-51` still tell a reader to give each vault its own Anki profile, `:52-55`
still describes the fix as a field holding the directory NAME, and `:830-834` still describes it as
a `vault::` TAG. `plan/Executor.scala:85` still carries "AND IT IS VAULT-BLIND, WHICH IS WHY ONE
PROFILE HOLDS ONE VAULT". All four need to follow.

STILL OPEN, and not settled by this ruling: adding a vault level moves every card already in a
collection. Scheduling survives a deck move, but two consequences do not follow the cards — Anki's
per-deck options presets stay with the old deck, so study limits silently reset, and a card sitting
in a filtered deck during the run is untested behaviour (`oas-n5n`, deferred, though the drill
binding creates one).
title: A collection cannot tell one vault's cards from another's

description:
The documentation tree is 20 files and 7,610 lines, and nobody can say what in it is still
outstanding. Things done are still written as todo, things abandoned read as planned, and work
that is genuinely open is stated only in prose that no query can find. This epic empties the
documents of their work items so that beads holds the status and the documents hold only
reasoning — which is what docs/README.md already says the arrangement is.

ONE SUB-EPIC PER FILE, and the extracted items are its children. Grouping by source file is the
point: a reader can ask what a document produced, and a document's own `bd list --spec` line then
answers "what is outstanding here" without the document saying anything that can go stale.

SCOPE, AND THE ORDER. reference/, design/ and findings/ first — 12 files, 3,478 lines. history/
is 4,067 lines and 53% of the tree, and by docs/README.md's own rules it is stale by definition;
it gets one cheap pass at the end asking ONLY whether it holds work nothing tracks, never
auditing its claims.

WHAT COUNTS AS A CANDIDATE. A document does not say "TODO". It says the tool cannot yet do X, or
to revisit before Y, or — the dangerous shape — states a plan in the present tense as though it
were built. Named shapes beat a keyword sweep.

EVERY CANDIDATE IS TRIAGED BEFORE IT REACHES A BEAD. Four outcomes, and only one is a task:
already built (the document is stale), already tracked (the document duplicates a bead),
genuinely outstanding (file it), abandoned (delete the line, do not file it). Skipping this step
reproduces the mess in a new format — which is how the mess was made.

DATES SETTLE CONFLICTS, NOT STATUS. Where two documents disagree, the later line usually wins.
But a recent line is not evidence that work is undone: a dated correction box found on
2026-08-31 was already false. The stronger signal is the GAP — a claim from February that the
code has since moved past is abandoned, not pending. Use `git log --follow -L` on the line range
rather than `git blame`, because several of these files were bulk-rewritten recently
(CLOZE-REDESIGN.md cut from 598 lines, EVOLVABILITY.md from 567) and blame dates every line to
the rewrite, which erases exactly that signal.
design:
METHOD, SETTLED 2026-08-31.

TWO AGENTS PER FILE, SEQUENTIAL RATHER THAN PARALLEL. The first extracts. The second is given
that list and asked what it missed — and is free to REJECT an item as already built, already
tracked, or not a claim about work at all. Sequential makes the second pass adversarial instead
of duplicative: it cannot produce the easy hits, so it has to look where the first did not. Two
parallel extractors overlap by most of their output and cost twice.

The pair passes are recorded in each file sub-epic's NOTES, not as beads. "Pass 1 found nine,
pass 2 added two and rejected one as already built" is provenance worth keeping; it is not work
anyone will do, and filing it would put method in a tracker meant for artifacts.

REPORT-ONLY. Agents do not edit. Correcting the documents is a separate phase, deliberately
deferred — see COMMENTS-BLOAT-REDUCTION-METHOD.md, which found that the documents largely
duplicate the code comments, so correcting them first polishes text that is about to change.

ABANDONED ITEMS COME BACK AS A DELETE LIST, NOT AS LOW-PRIORITY BEADS. Filing dead work is how
the original mess was made.

description:
VERIFIED from code. docs/findings/EVOLVABILITY.md records ONE trigger for an unlabelled cloze group's ordinal moving: an earlier highlight being inserted. Cloze.number builds its label set from every explicit label in the scope, groups by first appearance, and assigns each unlabelled group the lowest number no label claims. So the ordinal also moves when an earlier unlabelled highlight is DELETED, when highlights are REORDERED, when a LABEL IS ADDED anywhere with a number at or below the count of unlabelled groups, and when a LABEL IS REMOVED.

The last two are the alarming ones, because THE DOCUMENTED REMEDY IS ITSELF A TRIGGER. Given ==<<a>>== ==<<b>>==, a is c1 and b is c2. The author follows the tool's own printed advice — extract/Extractor.scala literally suggests writing a label — and writes ==<<2|a>>==. Now the label set is {2}, so a takes c2 and b takes c1: THE TWO CARDS SWAP CONTENT WHILE THE KEY IS UNTOUCHED. Nothing distinguishes that from a typo fix: the ordinals live inside the Text field, the content hash digests the whole field, the key never moves, and the planner emits an ordinary field update.

And the tool displays a group's current ordinal NOWHERE, so an author cannot choose the number that would make the edit free.

The cheapest half of a remedy needs no new Anki call: print each cloze unit's card count and each group's current ordinal and text. That data already exists in CardSpec.Cloze.deletions, which is built in extract/Cloze.scala and read by nothing in production.

The Anki half is UNVERIFIED and cannot be settled by reading: whether updateNoteFields re-points existing cloze cards at new content for their ordinal or regenerates them is decided inside Anki's compiled backend.

---

RECOVERED 2026-09-01 FROM `docs/reference/CARD-MODEL.md`, which lost it on 2026-08-31 when its
cloze section was rewritten rather than patched. It survived nowhere else in the repository.

**The hazard is not this project's discovery, and the corroboration is worth keeping.** From the
document, written 2026-08-19: *"Anki numbers cloze cards `c1…cn` and schedules each independently;
with positional numbering, deleting a middle deletion renumbers everything after it and scheduling
history moves between cards. That failure is documented in Yanki's manual as a known hazard."*

Two things follow. Another tool in this space met the same wall and wrote it down, so the failure
mode is established rather than theoretical — worth citing if anyone proposes positional numbering
again. And the design's answer to it, explicit grouping, was added on 2026-08-19 for reasons also
now recovered here: *"a sentence may hold ten highlights forming three groups — say 3, 3 and 4 —
and nothing could express that. Keying by text alone also had no answer for two identical
highlights in one section, or for what happens to a card's history when a typo inside a deletion is
fixed. Grouping dissolves all three."*

Which sharpens what this bead is about: grouping was adopted to stop ordinals drifting, and the
drift it did not close is the one an author causes by taking the tool's own advice.
title: The cloze ordinal-drift trigger set is wider than recorded, and the documented remedy is one of the triggers
